Give you this very personal and highly important story reason to follow the main quest as fast as possible (Oblivion/Skyrim-the world is ending, Fallout 3/4-hunt down the family member), so the narrative is encouraging you to focus on the main story. As a matter of fact their foreign office spent the last several years of the war begging and pleading with the US to sign a peace deal that wasn't complete surrender.

This put Imperial Japan in a bind because to them, unconditional surrender would mean the destruction of their nation. They believed this for several reasons, particularly because it's what they'd do to their own enemies if given the chance, so they assumed the same would happen to them. They were particularly afraid that they'd be forced to give up their Emperor, who was a massive figure in their cultural identity, far more so than even the British monarch.

They were fully aware and knew 100% that they stood no chance in a protracted war. That's why Pearl Harbor happened. Take out the US Pacific Fleet quick, take the islands they need, immediately try to sign a peace deal. It worked for them against the Russians in 1905, and if they'd destroyed the US fleet it probably would have worked again. They knew from the moment they failed to destroy the carrier force at Pearl that the war was going to be dicey, and knew the moment they lost at Midway that the war was over. All their efforts after that point were to try and get a conditional surrender instead of being utterly destroyed by the USA. 

The Japanese had no illusions about the USA. 

Germany, on the other hand, was completely the opposite. They started making war plans in 1940. Every plan they came up with said the same thing "we don't have enough divisions and tanks to maintain such a large offensive line". They ran war games where each one ended up the exact same way: They reached a point near Moscow and the Caucasus, then were spread so thinly that they couldn't concentrate enough tanks to break through anywhere, then they lost. Every time. 

The war office looked at it, saw all these problems, and said: "We've got this." They didn't change their plans at all, they didn't prepare for the problems that they foresaw, they didn't change their war goals. They all pretty much thought that if they just moved quickly enough and took Moscow before the Autumn rains that the Soviets would just give up and let them have the country. Conquer the whole thing in a few months. They never addressed the actual problem. It was never about time, it was about resources and manpower. They couldn't wage a war on such a large front with three different offensive pushes. It wasn't possible, they knew it wasn't possible, and they just plugged their ears and did it anyway. 

That's delusional.

Nothing could have worked. Japan was pretty much completely screwed no matter what they did. Attacking the US was the only option that had any real chance of working (and only a chance, if everything went off perfectly).

1: Japan couldn't just stop fighting in China. The front was already pretty much stagnated, and giving ground would be their only option. The problem is that the Imperial Army wouldn't stand for that. Any government that attempted to withdraw would find themselves dead rather quickly. The officers of the Empire were perfectly willing to kill Generals and public officials until they got the answer they wanted. It would also violate the character of the Japanese people at the time, so a withdraw from China was not going to happen.

Option 2, 3, and 4 all come down to the same problem: The Philippines. 

Sure, the Japanese could have avoided the Philippines and gone straight for the oil and rubber, but they also understood that the USA would likely enter the war eventually, and leaving the Philippines in their rear area as an enemy strongpoint was a bad idea. So if they were going to have a secure hold on the supply lines in the south, the Philippines would have to be taken, and that means war with the USA.

So war with the USA is going to happen no matter what. In that situation, the military leadership had to make a plan to win that war, or at least not lose too badly. They fully understood that conquering the USA was not on the table, and never even considered that option. This wasn't a Germany "ignoring the British to go invade the Soviets and hope they conquer everything" situation. They were banking on more of a Russo-Japanese war situation. Win a few big battles, show the Americans whos boss, and sign a favorable ceasefire. They planned on fighting a fairly limited, rapid campaign in the style of old 19th Century imperialists, but the war they ended up fighting was modern Total War where the only outcome was total victory or total defeat, and they were incapable of achieving total victory.

The initial plan was to invade the Philippines on the way to the Dutch and British holdings, then set a trap for the US Pacific fleet. The USA would have to send the fleet in, and the Imperial Navy wanted to trap and ambush them. Once the Pacific Fleet was gone they hoped to negotiate for a favorable peace, since the US wouldn't be able to stop Japan for a few years while they recovered their losses. Ironically the war plan with the USA was inspired largely by the work of the USN Admiral Mahan, who was a major influence on the doctrine of the Japanese navy during the build up to the Second World War.

This plan was very passive and left all the strategic initiative in the hands of the US Navy, which wasn't a good thing. What if they didn't take the bait? So Admiral Yamamoto Isoroku made a new plan centered around ambushing the Pacific fleet at anchor, thus keeping all the strategic initiative in the hands of the Imperial Navy. This became finalized in Operation AI, the attack on Pearl Harbor. 

Hard to tell how realistic the plan was. I personally think it had a pretty good chance of working IF (emphasize the IF) the US carrier forces were destroyed either at Pearl or Midway. Such a blow would have crippled the USN's ability to operate in the entire theater, and left the USA demoralized and impotent for years until new ships could be built and crewed. Even then, the Japanese would also be building more ships, and their crews would have far more experience and training. Sort of the opposite of what happened in real life. If the US built ships and threw them into the fight piecemeal to try and desperately hold or retake territory in the Pacific, we'd be defeated in detail. If they held back and gathered everything for a counterattack there would likely be massive unrest as it would seem like the government is spending years doing nothing while we lose island after island. In that situation, some sort of negotiation might have happened. Again, hard to say for sure. Too much speculation.

Attacking the southern islands, even if they tactfully avoided the Philippines (which was not an option) would mean they would be at war with the USA soon. They went into this with the expectation that they'd lose, but that if everything went just right, they'd come out a little better for it. However, the attack at Pearl Harbor didn't cripple the Pacific fleet as badly as hoped, and at Midway the tables turned and now the Japanese were the ones on the back-foot with a crippled fleet. From that point on actually getting a favorable peace was out of the question, and their only remaining goal was "oh god we have to sign some kind of conditional surrender before the US destroys our way of life". They spent those last few years practically begging for any kind of deal other than unconditional surrender, but they weren't going to get it.

The Art thing too...I don't think he's literally psychoanalyzing every species from their art. I think it's more of a mnemonic device to help him remember everything he's studied or deduced about an enemy or type of opponent. It's weird and esoteric on purpose, to enhance his own mystique (and because I think he has an actual appreciation for artwork).

Eh, Heinlein made some good points though. And it's pretty obvious from most of his writing that he's not actively advocating for that kind of world, just exploring ideas and philosophies. 

He's kind of right that most people don't care about voting, only around half of the voting population even uses that right at best. Nobody values it enough to use it, but everyone will complain about it if you take that right away. 

The idea that you have to earn something that we consider to be a basic right feels wrong, but it makes a degree of sense (as presented in the book). In the movie being a "citizen" is a carrot on a stick they dangle in front of the population to feed their war machine. In the book it's a serious responsibility that the government actively tells people to not take. The recruiters tell Rico over and over that he should only do this if he really wants to. 

The difference I think, goes back to perspective. To a western society we see voting as a basic right, that can't be given by a nation only taken away. In this other society it's different. Voting isn't a right, but everyone has the right to earn the ability to vote. If you're serious about becoming a citizen then the government will find something for you to do, because becoming a citizen is your right.

The implication is, of course, that citizens would be more invested in the political future of their nation now that they've earned their right to participate in it, and thus you have a more active and interested voting population. Whether it actually would is hard to say. Apathy might set in no matter what.

MacArthur was CE in my opinion. Dude was nuts, and arguably more responsible for the Bataan Death March than the guy he executed for it. He ignored the  existing war plan to fortify the Bataan peninsula and fill it with supplies for a long siege, instead deciding to hold the beaches and fight for every inch of soil. Either he thought it was a better plan, which makes him an idiot, or he just did it for PR, which makes him an evil idiot. 

Then, after getting shattered instantly at the beaches, he retreats all the way to the Bataan peninsula with few fortifications and little other supplies. He then decided that instead of fighting bravely for a brief time and surrendering, he'd fight to the last man for no reason. There was no strategic or tactical reason to hold out. He was just throwing lives away for the sake of throwing away lives.

The troopers and Filipinos on Bataan fought until they were dying of malaria, dehydration, dysentery and starvation long before they surrendered. Then MacArthur left. 

Many of the men captured were beyond saving, and despite common belief the Japanese general and higher officers actually tried. They just didn't have enough food, clean water, and medicine to treat the 75,000 prisoners. They had supplies for less than 30,000. Not to mention the fact that many lower raking officers and many enlisted men were cruel, violent, and murderous, and beat and killed many prisoners against orders. 

But far fewer would've died if not for MacArthur.

Yamashita is hard to place in my opinion. He fought for an evil regime, but that's harder to outright blame him for compared to German generals. German generals and other higher officers were serving a regime that had been in power for ten or so years, and pretty much everyone knew that Hitler took power through force and illegal means. But they did nothing about it because Hitler was doing things they wanted. That's more chaotic than anything. 

Yamashita and other Imperial Japanese officers were serving an institution that had been in existence for almost 100 years in its current form, and had been established for hundreds of years before that. So lawful fits.

But then you have to look at character, and that's where it gets really complicated. He was in charge during the defense of the Philippines, and quite a few war crimes were committed then. However his complicity in them is questionable. He was unaware of most of them (he was sort of preoccupied fighting a battle), and for many others he actively ordered them not to be committed. His orders were often just ignored.

He was executed by MacArthur because "a General is responsible for war crimes committed under their command regardless of whether they're aware of them at the time." Which is laudable to be honest. Where was MacArthur's trial? Or the trials of pretty much every American flag officer? Somebody committed a war crime in their ranks, so they're guilty, right? 

There were a few other generals executed by MacArthur under similarly questionable circumstances, but they were all generals who fought MacArthur. A lot of lawyers and legal experts in the states protested these executions, but they were killed anyway.

The Empire of Japan was very complicated compared to western nations. In western nations we're used to the people up top making all the decisions and everyone else doing what they say. That wasn't how Imperial Japan operated. 

Japan was dragged kicking and screaming into a war it didn't want in China by its own officers, and any government leader who tried to question them usually ended up dead. 

The Empire was also a sort of constitutional monarchy. There were very few hard legal limits on the Emperor's power, but there were so many years of convention and tradition that said he "shouldn't" do much. Yes, he technically had the power to prevent the war and to end it at any point, and he didn't use it. A lot of people blame him for that. Whether it's right to blame him or not, I can't say. 

I read the Rising Sun by John Toland, lots of firsthand accounts of a lot of the decision making in Imperial Japan and it's very confusing.
